paras: The expulsion of Black workers from the Evansville and Princeton traction line took place on June 3, 1903, when white workers drove thirty Black laborers from a construction job on the company's traction line in Gibson County, Indiana. The Black men were ordered out of the county and were allowed back only under an arrangement with the contractor that barred them from any work white men wanted. Southern papers picked up the Indianapolis dispatch and used it to argue that the North was hostile to Black workers.

The thirty Black workers were employed on the traction line being built by the Evansville and Princeton Company in Gibson County. According to the dispatch, they had been sent to unload crushed stone, while white workers had been left to do the heavier work of grading.

The white teamsters on the job refused to haul the stone the Black men unloaded. Whites then drove the Black workers from their work, claiming that they were doing work that should be done by white men. The Black men were ordered out of the county and left. No injuries are reported, and the dispatch names neither the workers nor anyone who drove them off.

The workers later returned under an arrangement with the contractor by which they were not to do any work that white men wanted to do. Notices were posted informing everyone of the agreement and warning the Black workers not to violate it. No report of arrests or of any official response appears in the coverage, and no later account of whether the agreement held was found.

The story reached print as a single Indianapolis wire dispatch. The Evening Times-Republican of Marshalltown, Iowa, ran it on its front page on June 4 under the headline 'Drive Negro Laborers Away' and the deck 'Whites Force Contractor to Allow Them to Choose Their Work.' Most of the other printings found were in Southern papers, which gave it a sharper edge.

The Weekly Corinthian of Corinth, Mississippi, printed the wire on June 9 under the headline 'Heinous Crime. White People in Indiana Drive Out Negroes.' The next day the Montgomery Advertiser quoted the dispatch in full inside an editorial attacking a proposed movement of Black migrants to Boston, presenting it as 'fairly indicative of the good time ahead for the negroes who go North and West seeking to make an honest living.' The Water Valley Progress in Mississippi paraphrased the story on June 13, calling it an 'outrage' that would have raised 'a howl of indignation through the width and breadth of Yankeedom' had it occurred in the South.

A version credited to the Chicago Record-Herald ran under the heading 'No Use for Negroes' in the Batesburg Advocate of South Carolina on June 17 and twice in the Marlboro Democrat of Bennettsville, South Carolina, on June 19. No report of the episode was found in the Black press or in a local Gibson County paper.

Most versions place the expulsion on Wednesday, June 3, but the Montgomery Advertiser described the dispatch as dated June 5 while keeping its word 'yesterday', which would put the event a day later. The Water Valley Progress described the men as throwing up dirt for a railroad bed near Evansville rather than unloading stone in Gibson County, a looser paraphrase without a dateline.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black workers from the Evansville and Princeton traction line
bases: White workers drove thirty Black laborers off a construction job on the claim that the work should be theirs, then forced a contractor's agreement limiting what work Black men could do (A2, A3, A4).

Every report traces to one Indianapolis wire dispatch, reprinted or paraphrased (A2, A3, A4, A6) or loosely summarized in editorial comment (A5); no local or independent account and no Black-press report was found.

accounts.label: Indianapolis wire report
accounts.gist: Thirty Black workers sent to unload crushed stone were driven off by whites who said the work should be theirs; white teamsters refused to haul the stone; the Black men were ordered out of the county, left, and returned under a contractor's arrangement, with notices posted.

accounts.label: Water Valley Progress editorial paraphrase
accounts.gist: About thirty Black men throwing up dirt for a new railroad bed near 'Evainsville' were driven off by 'a gang of white men who wanted their jobs'.

framing.detail: The Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican ran the dispatch on page one as 'DRIVE NEGRO LABORERS AWAY. Whites Force Contractor to Allow Them to Choose Their Work.'
The Weekly Corinthian headlined the wire 'HEINOUS CRIME. White People in Indiana Drive Out Negroes.'
The Montgomery Advertiser quoted the dispatch in an editorial against Black migration to Boston as 'fairly indicative of the good time ahead' for Black migrants going North.
The Water Valley Progress called it an 'outrage' that would have raised 'a howl of indignation' in 'Yankeedom' had it happened in the South.
The Batesburg Advocate and Marlboro Democrat ran the Chicago Record-Herald version under 'No Use for Negroes'.
